issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not replace a subordinate authority’s supported factual finding merely because it would assess the evidence differently.
material_facts: The Appellate Authority considered the pleadings and evidence and found that the landlord had established a bona fide need for personal occupation.
The High Court set aside that finding after reassessing the evidence and drawing different inferences from the landlord’s living arrangements and the condition of the building.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the proper limits of revisional review by reassessing evidence that supported the Appellate Authority’s finding; that finding was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965, revisional jurisdiction is wider than the jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC but is not an appeal. It is essentially supervisory, and a revisional court should not independently reassess evidence or supplant a supported factual conclusion. The Court relied on Dattonpant Gopalvarao Devakate v. Vithabrao Maruthirao Janagaval, M/s. Sri Raja Lakshmi Dyeing Works v. Rangaswamy Chettiar, and Rajbir v. S. Chokesiri & Co.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision concerning a rent-control decision.
predicates.subordinate_factual_finding_supported_by: The subordinate authority’s factual finding is supported by evidence on the record.
predicates.revisional_court_reassessed_evidence_to_: The revisional court independently reassessed the evidence and reached a different factual view.

issues.definition: When a supported factual finding in a rent-control matter is challenged through revision, reassessment to reach a different view does not permit the revisional court to substitute its own factual conclusion.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s bona fide claim to occupy a building is not defeated solely because the landlord lives in a relative’s house or the building requires repairs or alterations before occupation.
material_facts: The landlord was living in a house belonging to his son and claimed that he wished to live in a house of his own.
The rented building lacked some residential facilities and required repairs or alterations, but the evidence indicated it could be made suitable for residence.
The Appellate Authority found the landlord’s personal-occupation need bona fide, and the Supreme Court restored that finding.
issues.conclusion: Neither the landlord’s residence in his son’s house nor the need for repairs or alterations justified rejecting the bona fide need for personal occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965 does not require a landlord to occupy a building without making alterations. The Court approved Devaky v. Krishnankutty and relied on Ramniklal Pitambardas Mehta v. Indradaman Amratlal Sheth for the principle that intended alterations do not, by themselves, affect a bona fide requirement for occupation.

predicates.personal_residence_eviction_claim: A landlord seeks possession of a rented building for the landlord’s own residence.
predicates.landlord_lives_in_a_relative_house: The landlord currently resides in a house belonging to a relative.
predicates.premises_need_repairs_or_alterations: The rented building requires repairs or alterations before it can be used for residence.

issues.definition: In a claim for possession for the landlord’s own residence, living in a relative’s house or needing to repair or alter the rented building, by itself, does not negate bona fide need.

issues.legal_issue: Before ordering eviction for a landlord’s bona fide need, the appellate authority must determine whether the tenant qualifies for protection based on dependence on the business income and the availability of other suitable premises.
material_facts: The landlord’s eviction claim for personal occupation was accepted by the Appellate Authority.
The Rent Controller had observed that the tenant depended on income from the business in the building, but had not made a definite finding on the availability of other suitable premises.
The Appellate Authority did not consider whether the tenant qualified for the protection, and the Supreme Court remanded the matter for that determination.
issues.conclusion: The matter had to be remanded to the Appellate Authority to determine whether the tenant could invoke the protection against eviction.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965 prevents an eviction order where the tenant depends mainly for a livelihood on trade or business carried on in the building and no other suitable building is available in the locality. The authority must consider whether those conditions are met before ordering eviction on the ground of bona fide need.

predicates.bona_fide_need_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction on the ground that the landlord bona fide needs the building for occupation.
predicates.tenant_mainly_depends_on_business_income: The tenant mainly depends for a livelihood on income from trade or business carried on in the building.
predicates.alternative_premises_availability_unreso: It remains undetermined whether another suitable building is available locally for the tenant’s trade or business.
predicates.appellate_authority_skipped_tenant_prote: The appellate authority ordered eviction without determining whether the tenant qualifies for protection based on livelihood dependence and the availability of other suitable premises.

issues.definition: When a tenant’s livelihood dependence and the availability of alternative premises remain relevant but unresolved, an eviction decision made without reviewing that protection must be remanded for its determination.
